# Swarm Intelligence for Predicting Software Development Effort

YENNY VILLUENDAS-REY 1, CUAUHTÉMOC LÓPEZ-MARTÍN 2,
JOSÉ LUIS VELÁZQUEZ-RODRÍGUEZ 3, AND CORNELIO YÁÑEZ-MÁRQUEZ 3

1 Centro de Innovación y Desarrollo Tecnológico en Cómputo, Instituto Politécnico Nacional, Mexico City 07700, Mexico
2 Department of Information Systems, Universidad de Guadalajara, Guadalajara 44100, Mexico
3 Centro de Investigación en Computación, Instituto Politécnico Nacional, Mexico City 07738, Mexico

Corresponding authors: Yenny Villuendas-Rey (yvilluendasr@ipn.mx) and Cornelio Yáñez-Márquez (coryanez@gmail.com)

**ABSTRACT** An accurate development effort prediction (measured in person-hours) of a software project
remains a challenge in the software engineering management field, due to either under-prediction or overprediction negatively affecting the budgeting and resource allocation to be assigned to the project. Hundreds
of studies have explored software development effort prediction models; however, only a limited number
of them have applied metaheuristic techniques to optimize the parameters of statistical regression equations
(SREs). In addition, most algorithms require a huge amount of data to successfully learn the underlying
model parameters. Accordingly, we introduce a novel variant of a swarm intelligence algorithm termed
*Mexican Axolotl Optimization* (MAO), designed for optimizing the SRE parameters and for selecting the
SRE within a unified optimization framework. Our approach enables the simultaneous identification of
the most suitable SRE model and its optimal configuration, thereby enhancing predictive accuracy. Our
proposal was evaluated on eight data sets of software projects selected from an international public repository.
The performance of our proposal, named MAO-SRE, is compared to that obtained from traditional SRE,
multilayer perceptron neural networks, support vector regression, random forest, and SREs optimized
through particle swarm optimization and genetic algorithms. Results based on statistical significance allow
us to conclude that MAO-SRE can be used to predict the development effort of software projects, considering
their development type, development platform, and programming language generation.

**INDEX TERMS** Statistical regression, software effort prediction, software engineering, swarm intelligence
algorithms.


**I. INTRODUCTION**

Software development effort prediction (SDEP) belongs to
software project planning, which corresponds to an activity
of software engineering management [1]. It is useful for managers for budgeting software projects. The effort is reported
in person-hours [2], and the project size has commonly been
used as the explanatory variable for the SDEP. Source lines of
code and function points have been the types of size majorly
used [2].
Both cost over-prediction and cost under-prediction affect
the planning of software projects. Therefore, an accurate
SDEP is needed. The importance of SDEP has been reflected

The associate editor coordinating the review of this manuscript and

approving it for publication was Anandakumar Haldorai .


in the publication of several systematic reviews between
2007 and 2025, where hundreds of studies on SDEP have
been analyzed [2], [3], [4], [5], [6], [7], [8], [9], [10]. A diversity of SDEP techniques has been identified in the mentioned
reviews, usually divided into mathematical models and nonmathematical models. In the first type mentioned, the models
can be subclassified into statistical regression models and
machine learning models, including Deep Learning techniques [11], [12]. Their parameters have been optimized (i.e.,
feature weighting) by applying metaheuristic algorithms.
Optimization algorithms remain in use in the software
engineering area [13], [14], [15], [16], following their application more than twenty years ago, when a study concluded
that there was excellent potential for exploiting metaheuristics in certain software engineering areas, such as effort


2025 The Authors. This work is licensed under a Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 License.
207448 For more information, see https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/ VOLUME 13, 2025

Y. Villuendas-Rey et al.: Swarm Intelligence for Predicting Software Development Effort


prediction [17]. Thus, we follow the recommendation of the
mentioned study, whose goal was to stimulate more interest
in using metaheuristics for finding near-optimal solutions in
the software engineering field.
Figure 1 illustrates the software development process
phases for which effort will be predicted. The components
by phase are the following [18]:

  - Design: External design and internal design.

  - Construction: Construct code, review or inspect, interfaces, unit test, and integrate software.

  - Testing: System testing, performance testing, automated
tests, and acceptance testing.

  - Implementation: Releases for delivery, install software
releases for users, user documentation, deliver user
training, and provide user support.
Metaheuristic algorithms have been classified as swarm
intelligence (simulating the behavior of animals and insects
in their environment), evolutionary (that are inspired by
evolutionary principles in nature and among living creatures), physics-based (which simulates the physical laws),
and human-based algorithms (simulating the behavior and
laws of human societies) [19].
We have identified several metaheuristic algorithms used
for feature weighting in prediction models applied to SDEP in
the past 25 years. Our research question is the following: How
can the development effort prediction accuracy of software
projects be improved by using a new swarm intelligence
metaheuristic algorithm for optimizing the statistical model
selection and its parameters?

**FIGURE 1.** Development phases of a software project.

In the present study, we apply a novel swarm intelligence
metaheuristic algorithm, the Mexican Axolotl Optimization


algorithm (MAO) [20]. MAO has been successfully applied
to several optimization tasks, including vehicle parking [21],
power scheduling [22], and network control [23].
Our proposal specially modifies MAO for SDEP. The motivation to design a novel representation of solutions and novel
searching operators in the context of a novel MAO-based
algorithm is supported by the following issues:

1) A significant finding in a recent systematic review of
the literature on SDEP is that it is not possible to state
that any SDEP model is the most promising based on
the same data set and accuracy aspects [2].
2) We identified thirty metaheuristic algorithms in the
[twenty-eight SDEP studies (Appendix, and none of](app:1#A.I.))
them apply MAO.
3) Only nine of the twenty-eight studies apply metaheuristics for optimizing the parameters of statistical
equations.
4) There is a need to optimize not only the parameters of
statistical regression equations (SRE) but also to embed
the selection of the SRE model in the optimization
algorithm.

Regarding data sets, prediction accuracy measures, and validation methods, our study presents several advantages.
We use the International Software Benchmarking Standards
Group (ISBSG) release 2018, which is an international public
repository commonly used in the software engineering field
when development effort has been predicted [24]. The data
sets were selected observing the ISBSG guidelines, that is,
based on the quality of data, type of development, development platform, programming language generation, and
resource level (i.e., how the effort was quantified) [25].
In addition, we measure the performance of the models
based on absolute residuals (a non-biased measure [26]),
and we used the leave-one-out cross-validation procedure
because it is a deterministic procedure that can be exactly
reproduced by other researchers [2]. It uses mutually exclusive data sets for training and testing the models, leading to
stability by removing the random selection of data sets. The
main contributions of our study are:

1) The proposal of a novel MAO-SRE optimization
algorithm able to simultaneously optimize the selection
of a suitable SRE model, as well as its parameters in
the same optimization procedure. MAO-SRE is based
on MAO and preserves its advantages of having high
exploration and exploitation capabilities.
2) The proposal of a novel representation of solutions in
the context of optimizing SRE parameters, allowing
solutions with variable length, and embedding the SRE
model in the optimization procedure.
3) The proposal of novel exploration and exploitation
operators for variable-length solutions based on the
MAO operators.
4) Our proposal predicts the number of person-hours
(effort) needed to complete a software project accurately than others in the state-of-the-art.

Y. Villuendas-Rey et al.: Swarm Intelligence for Predicting Software Development Effort


The remainder of this study is structured as follows: Section II
describes related studies that have applied metaheuristic algorithms for feature weighting in SDEP models. Section III
describes our proposal: the MAO-SRE. Section IV details the
models used for comparison, their parameters, the selection
of the software project data sets, the validation techniques,
and the performance measures. Section V presents the
results of MAO-SRE with respect to other metaheuristic
and machine learning models. It also discusses the results
obtained from a statistical viewpoint and covers the limitations and validation threats of our study.
Finally, Section VI corresponds to our conclusions and
future work.

**II. RELATED WORKS**

Several recent machine learning approaches have been
used for effort prediction, including Deep Learning techniques [11], [12]. Since our study concerns feature weighting
in the SDEP field, we searched for studies on effort prediction
using metaheuristic algorithms (Appendix A.I). In accordance with our findings, the metaheuristic algorithms have
been used for optimizing several types of models:
1) Machine Learning

    - Adaptive Neuro-Fuzzy Inference System [27],

[28], [29].

    - Functional link neural network [36].

    - Multi-layer Perceptron neural network [19], [37],

[38].

    - Radial Basis Function neural network [36].

    - Support Vector Regression [39].

    - Wavelet neural network [40].

    - COCOMO II equation [41], [42], [43], [44]:
*Effort* = 2 *.* 9 *KLOC* [0] *[.]* [91], where *KLOC* corresponds
to thousands of source lines of code.

    - COCOMO 81 equation [45], [46], [47], [48]:

Building prediction models involves considering the factors that influence the software development process [2].
Metaheuristic algorithms have also been used to facilitate the
selection of software prediction models.
The metaheuristic reported as the most used in 2012 was
genetic algorithms [5], whereas in 2019, genetic algorithms,
PSO, and Tabu search were reported as the most used [7].
Most recently, a systematic literature review on SDEP ensemble models published in 2022 reports that a genetic algorithm
for the bagging M5Rule was the best method [9].

**III. NOVEL MEXICAN AXOLOTL ALGORITHM FOR THE**

**SELECTION AND OPTIMIZATION OF STATISTICAL**

**REGRESSION EQUATION**
In this section, we introduce a novel model for effort prediction based on the Mexican Axolotl Optimization (MAO)
algorithm. Subsection A refers to the main MAO characteristics, and subsection B explains the novel approach to
optimizing statistical regression equations for software prediction, named MAO-SRE.

*A. MEXICAN AXOLOTL OPTIMIZATION*

Axolotls are studied for their remarkable regeneration capabilities, including the repair of their spinal cord and complex
tissues such as retinal, restoring full functionalities in their
bodies. They also straightforwardly accept transplants from
other individuals, not only of extremities but all organs,
including the brain. In addition, axolotls can also change their
coloring to camouflage in the environment [54], [55].
Those abilities are mimicked in the Mexican Axolotl Optimization (MAO) algorithm, in which artificial axolotls are
able to camouflage in the environment, restore damaged parts
of their bodies, and reproduce to obtain new generations
of solutions. The particular characteristics of MAO make
it suitable for exploring huge areas of search spaces while
having fast convergence [16]. Figure 2 shows the results of
MAO for the numeric optimization function in (1).

*F (x)* = *g* ( *x* ) − *h* ( *x* ) + 20 + *e* (1)





~~�~~
�
�
�


The MAO algorithm, represented in pseudocode, is described
in [20].

**FIGURE 2.** Example of the results of MAO over the numeric function.
(a) Plotting of the function in a two-dimensional space. (b) Convergence
curve of MAO. Note that the best results are found before 50 evaluations.

Despite the advantages of MAO, it requires fixed-length
solutions (axolotls), as usual in metaheuristic algorithms.
That is, if we need to search for the optimal parameters of a
certain model (i.e., an SRE), we need to apply the algorithm
for the desired number of iterations. If we need to select

among several SREs (20 in this research), then we need
to apply the MAO twenty times, each time for the desired
number of iterations. Therefore, if we selected 200 iterations,

then we will need 20×200 =4000 iterations to obtain a result.

To overcome this problem, we introduced a new variant of
the original MAO described in [20] to optimize the SREs to
be applied for SDEP.

*B. MEXICAN AXOLOTL OPTIMIZATION FOR STATISTICAL*

*REGRESSION EQUATIONS*

The proposed Mexican Axolotl Optimization for Statistical
Regression Equations (MAO-SRE) includes two main modifications to the MAO algorithm. The first one is a novel
representation of the solutions that includes an additional
dimension for each axolotl, representing the SRE used by
the individual. The second one is to use a flexible number
of dimensions for each axolotl, depending on the number of
parameters the corresponding SRE needs, and to design novel
exploration and exploitation operators to travel the search
space, as well as a novel assortment operator. Accordingly,
we consider 20 possible SREs in this research, as described in

As shown, MAO converges near zero in less than 100 evaluations of the optimization function.
The selection of the Mexican Axolotl Optimization (MAO)
is supported by its amazing experimental results over benchmark optimization functions [16] and in solving real-world
problems [56], [57], [58].
Its main relevance for software effort prediction is its ability to traverse complex search spaces in a short number of
evaluations, combining exploration and exploitation of the
solutions in a very efficient way. In particular, it showed
better optimization capabilities than many well-established
optimization algorithms in composite optimization functions [16].
In MAO, the set of solutions (axolotls) of size *np* comprises the population *P* = � *S* 1 *, . . ., S* *np* � and each solution
(axolotl) *S* ∈ *P* is represented as a D-dimensional vector
of form *S* = [ *s* 1 *, . . ., s* *D* ], with min *i* ≤ *s* *i* ≤ max *i*, such
that *O* ( *S* ) ∈ *R* . We also assume a minimization problem.

**TABLE 3.** Statistical regression equations considered in the MAO-SRE.


Y. Villuendas-Rey et al.: Swarm Intelligence for Predicting Software Development Effort

**FIGURE 3.** Example of assortment in MAO-SRE.

Algorithm 1 presents the general pseudocode of the proposed MAO-SRE. Algorithm 2 presents the pseudocode
of the Transition procedure of the algorithms; Algorithm
3 presents the pseudocode for the Injury and Restoration
procedure, and Algorithm 4 shows the pseudocode for the
Crossover procedure.
As in [59], the novel assortment operator, as in
Algorithm 4, considers crossing individuals with different
numbers of dimensions (i.e., parents having SRE with a
different number of parameters). Our proposal still obtains
two eggs, one with the equation with fewer parameters and
the other with the equation with more parameters. We use
uniform crossover for the minimum number of parameters
for both eggs, and we complete the egg with more parameters
with the parent’s values, with the same parameter number.
The advantages of the proposed MAO-SRE are its ability
to handle variable-length solutions, to simultaneously select
the desired SRE, and to optimize its parameters in a single
procedure.


Table 3. However, the proposal allows the use of any number
of SREs.

Thus, to obtain the novel MAO-SRE, we were inspired by
the variable-length optimization strategy proposed in [59],
and modified the MAO algorithm as follows:

1) We transition the first dimension (corresponding to the
SRE number) by selecting a random number in [ *1,*
*ne* ], where *ne* is the number of SREs. We maintain the
transition equation for the remaining *D* dimensions.
2) We restore the first dimension by rounding the results
of the restoring equation to the next integer number in

[ *1, ne* ].
3) We design a novel assortment operator and modify
the assortment of individuals as follows: If the parents
have SRE with a different number of parameters (for
instance, equations 1 and 3), we will obtain two eggs,
one with the equation of the female and the other with
the equation of the male. We will use uniform crossover
for the minimum number of parameters for both eggs.
Then, for the egg with more parameters, we will use
the parent’s values with the same parameter number
(Figure 3).

These novel modifications described in Algorithms 1 to 4
(Figures 4-7) allow us to optimize simultaneously the SRE
to be selected, as well as its parameters. In addition, such
modifications are applicable to other SREs, not limited to the
ones in Table 3, which makes the novel MAO-SRE useful for
different scenarios involving the optimization of equations.


**FIGURE 4.** Algorithm 1. MAO-SRE.

For 20 SREs and 200 iterations, we can obtain the optimized solution in just 200 iterations, while the classic MAO
needs 20 × 200 = 4000 iterations. In addition, the proposed

**FIGURE 7.** Algorithm 4. New life (Assortment).


**FIGURE 5.** Algorithm 2. Transition from larva to adult.

**FIGURE 6.** Algorithm 3. Injury and Restoration.

MAO-SRE is not exclusive to statistical regression equations,
nor to SDEP. As a metaheuristic, it can be applied to any problem considering a set of possible functions (first dimension),
with a variable number of parameters by function, as long as
those variables are defined in the same interval.
Otherwise, the proposed assortment operator can return
invalid solutions. It is essential to mention that in our exper

iments, the assortment procedure does not produce invalid
solutions, because all statistical regression equations used are

−
defined in the same interval [ 10, 10].
We conducted an ablation study to analyze the effect of
population size and number of evaluations in the proposed
MAO-SRE. The results for population size and evaluation
number are in Appendix B. The study suggests that each
individual should have an average number of evaluations
between 10 and 50.

The following section presents the details regarding the
model training and data sets used.

**IV. PREDICTION MODELS AND SOFTWARE DATA SETS**

This section presents the prediction models used in this
research, as well as the selected data sets of software projects.
Additionally, it covers the validation procedures and performance measures that are analyzed.

*A. PREDICTION MODELS AND PARAMETERS*

In this study, we apply a novel MAO-based algorithm for
the parameter optimization of statistical regression equations
(SRE) employed in SDEP (referred to as MAO-SRE), including the selection of equations themselves. Each equation is
derived from a regression analysis. The optimization of SRE
is also based on those nine studies of Table 1, which involve
the optimization of the SRE parameters using a metaheuristic.
We tested three machine learning models and three
metaheuristic optimization algorithms, along with statistical regression. The selected machine learning models were
multilayer perceptron neural network (MLP), support vector
regression (SVR), and random forest (RF).
For MLP [60], we used a neural network with the following
architecture: an input layer, one hidden layer, and an output


VOLUME 13, 2025 207453

Y. Villuendas-Rey et al.: Swarm Intelligence for Predicting Software Development Effort


layer. The types of SVR we used were *ε* -SVR and *v* -SVR.
The *ε* -SVR performs prediction tasks from the *ε* -insensitive
loss function (i.e., the *ε* -SVR tolerates an absolute value of
at most *ε* for the difference between the actual value and

predicted value) [61], whereas the *v* -SVR minimizes the *ε* insensitive loss function and changes the SVR formulation
using a *v* parameter having a value between zero and one [62].
Sometimes, data are non-linearly separable, and a kernel
is used for a higher-dimensional space representation. Thus,
we used four types of kernels by type of SVR (linear, polynomial, radial basis function, and sigmoid) [63].
The small size of the data sets, the small number of parameters, and their limited range, as determined by the model
to be optimized, enabled an exhaustive search for optimal
MLP and SVR parameter values. Table 4 includes the optimal
values found for MLP and SVR by data set described in
‘‘B. Data sets of software projects’’ section, once a leaveone-out cross-validation was performed. Finally, the Random
Forest ensemble for regression had 100 base trees of 10-level
depth each. The metaheuristic algorithms evaluated along
with MAO were particle swarm optimization (PSO) [64]
and genetic algorithms (GA), both commonly used in SDEP
models (Appendix A.I).

**TABLE 4.** Optimal parameter values for MLP and SVR (NHL: number of
hidden layers; LR: Learning Rate; M: Momentum; SVRT: SVR type; KT:
Kernel type, PV: Parameter values).

**TABLE 5.** Metaheuristic algorithms applied in feature weighting of SDEP
models.


Several equations have been developed for particle updating [65], all accounting for the swarm’s individual and global
knowledge. Several variants of PSO have been introduced,
and PSO-SRE is one of them [49]. In addition, we also consider a version of GA to optimize the parameters of SRE by a
GA algorithm (hereafter termed GA-SRE). Table 5 presents
the parameters for MAO-SRE, PSO-SRE, and GA-SRE.
The criteria for selecting these models are the following:

1) The prediction accuracy of machine learning models
has mostly been compared to the SRE accuracy [5], [7].
2) The prediction accuracy of SRE has been reported as
better than that obtained from machine learning models [7].
3) Two systematic reviews of the literature published in
2012 [5] and 2019 [7] about SDEP have reported
the multilayer back-propagation neural network (MLP)
and the support vector regression (SVR) as the more
accurate machine learning models.
4) A new proposed SDEP model should at least outperform SRE [66].
5) The nine studies of Table 1 involved an SRE for comparing its performance to that of the new proposed
model.

6) In accordance with Appendix A, PSO and GA algorithms are the most used in the SDEP field.
7) The PSO-SRE [49] uses the same data sets, validation
method, and prediction accuracy criteria used in the
present study.

Thus, we observed the recommendations of a recent systematic literature review on SDEP studies [2], in the sense of
(1) using the same data sets, (2) using the same prediction
accuracy measure, and (3) training and testing the models
using the same validation method.

*B. DATA SETS OF SOFTWARE PROJECTS*

The algorithms in our study were trained and tested with data
sets obtained from the ISBSG release 2018, which contains
8,261 software projects developed between 1989 and 2016 in
32 countries [67]. The development platforms reported by the
ISBSG are multiplatform (Multi), personal computer (PC),
midrange (MR), and Mainframe (MF). The different types of
programming languages are considered as application generator, second (2GL), third (3GL), and fourth (4GL) generation.
The resource level is classified into four levels in accordance with the manner in which that effort is quantified (level
1 is used in our study, which corresponds to development
team effort). The data sets were selected observing the ISBSG
guidelines mentioned in Table 6, which are: taking into
account the quality of data, functional size method, type of
development, development platform, programming language
type, and resource level type [25].
Eight data sets involving 1,500 projects from the 2,054
projects of Table 7 were finally selected for our study. Data
sets of Table 7 were obtained based on the following data
preprocessing [49]:


207454 VOLUME 13, 2025

Y. Villuendas-Rey et al.: Swarm Intelligence for Predicting Software Development Effort



The quality data of projects ranges from ‘‘A’’ to ‘‘D’’ types.
The ‘‘A’’ and ‘‘B’’ were selected since they are recommended
by the ISBSG for statistical analysis [25].
The type of functional size method selected was IFPUG.
The pre-IFPUG V4 projects with V4 and post V4 should
not be merged (ISBSG, 2018b); thus, only projects with a
functional size method corresponding to IFPUG 4+ were
selected. The ISBSG reports the functional size method in
adjusted function points, a composite value computed from
nineteen variables. The unadjusted function points are calculated based on internal logical files, external interface
files, external inputs, external outputs, and external inquiries.
This value is then adjusted using fourteen variables: data
communications, distributed data processing, performance,
heavily used configuration, transaction rate, online data
entry, end-user efficiency, online update, complex processing,
reusability, installation ease, operational ease, multiple sites,
and facilitate change [68].
A scatter plot of the raw data set of Table 7 was generated
(Appendix C) to select the data sets according to the ISBSG
criteria. All of them showed skewness, heteroscedasticity, and
the presence of outliers. After applying the *χ* 2, Shapiro-Wilk,
skewness, and kurtosis statistical normality tests to *effort* and
*adjusted function points* variables, the hypothesis that *effort*
and *adjusted function points* come from a normal distribution
was rejected for all cases with 99% confidence. Thus, data
were normalized by applying the natural logarithm (ln) [66].

**TABLE 6.** Selection criteria for ISBSG Release 18 data sets.

**TABLE 7.** Data sets used for training and testing the MAO-SRE, SRE, MLP,
SVR, and PSO-SRE models (Type: type of development, Set: Data set
identifier, Plat: Development platform, Lang: Programming language type,
NSP: Number of Software Projects).

In each scatter plot containing transformed (i.e., normalized) data, outliers were identified based on studentized


residuals having an absolute value higher than 2.5. A 5%
of outliers by data set was the maximum acceptable [69].
A positive correlation coefficient was only acceptable if the
assumption of all equations coincided with the development
effort; that is, the larger the size, the higher the effort.
A minimum percentage of 50% for the coefficient of determination was used because it has been minimally accepted for
SDEP models [70]. Considering the characteristics described
above, we selected eight data sets (Table 7 ).

*C. VALIDATION AND PERFORMANCE*

We used the leave-one-out cross-validation (LOOCV) procedure for training and testing the models. Regarding performance, we compute absolute residuals (AR), which is a
symmetric measure and unbiased since it is not based on
ratios. The advantages of AR are that it provides an original
measure of the size of the prediction error, indicating how far
the prediction of the model is from the actual value, which
can make the error interpretation more intuitive. AR has been
recommended over other measures based on ratios such as the

magnitude of relative error, which has even been qualified
as ‘‘deprecated’’ [24]. Absolute Residuals are calculated as
follows [49]:

AR *i* = |ActualEffort *i* − PredictedEffort *i* | (4)

An absolute residual is calculated for each software project
*i* . The mean (MAR) of multiple software projects n is
obtained as:

MAR = �1� *n* � [�] AR *i* (5)

The MdAR represents the median of the ARs. We also
used standardized accuracy (SA) to determine if the modelperforms better than random estimating Po, where *MAR* ¯ *Po*
is the mean value of a large number of runs of random
guessing [26]:

*SA* = 1 − *[MAR]* ¯ ∗ 100 (6)

*MAR* *Po*

Finally, we applied the effect size ( *�* ) measure considering
*S* *Po* as the sample standard deviation of the random guessing
strategy. A *�* value larger than or equal to 0.5 is recommended for good predictions.

*MAR* ¯ *Po*
*�* = *[MAR]* [ −] (7)
*S* *Po*

The explanatory variable used is the size represented in
adjusted function points, whose value is calculated from nineteen explanatory variables mentioned in the ‘‘B. Data sets of
software projects’’ subsection.

**V. RESULTS, DISCUSSION, AND VALIDITY**
We present the numerical results of the compared models
through a leave-one-out cross-validation on the eight selected
data sets. Then, we discuss the proposed research hypothesis by statistical analysis and finally present some validity
threads for the research.


VOLUME 13, 2025 207455

*A. NUMERICAL RESULTS*

(MAR, MdAR, SA, and *�* ) for the seven compared models

Tables 8-11 include the MAR, MdAR, SA, and *�* results
obtained once the models were applied to the eight data sets,
respectively.
In addition, we analyzed the execution time of the
compared algorithms (Table 12). As shown, the complete
LOOCV procedure was performed in less than a minute for
the biggest data set. The proposed model has execution times
similar to those of GA-SRE and PSO-SRE. The fastest model

was SRE, and the slowest were MLP and RF.

than that recommended (0.5), then the application of any of

*B. DISCUSSION*

We obtained the ARs of MAO-SRE and the ARs of each

prediction model to conduct a statistical analysis by data
set. Then, we analyzed whether the data were normally distributed. The *χ* [2], Shapiro-Wilk, skewness, and kurtosis tests
of normality were performed (Appendix C.I ). As shown,
at least one model by data set does not follow a normal distribution. Therefore, we conclude that non-parametric statistical
analysis is better suited for our data (Table 14). Accordingly,
we used a combination of the Friedman test for comparing
*k* related samples, followed by a post hoc test to mitigate
inflated Type I error.
We selected a significance level of 0.05 for a 95% confidence, and for each data set, we tested the following null (H 0 )
and alternative (H 1 ) hypotheses with adjusted function points
as the explanatory variable:


207456 VOLUME 13, 2025

Y. Villuendas-Rey et al.: Swarm Intelligence for Predicting Software Development Effort


**TABLE 14.** Statistical tests for the compared models.

H 0 : The predictive accuracy of MAO-SRE is statistically
equal to that of SRE, MLP, SVR, RF, GA-SRE, and PSO-SRE
for predicting the development effort of software projects.


H 1 : The predictive accuracy of MAO-SRE is statistically
not equal to that of SRE, MLP, SVR, RF, GA-SRE, and
PSO-SRE for predicting the development effort of software
projects.
The Friedman test rejected the null hypothesis for all data
sets with p-values lower than 0.0000, and we conducted the
corresponding post hoc analysis using Holm’s test.
Table 14 presents the results for Friedman’s ranking as
well as Holm’s post hoc statistical comparison between the
best-ranked algorithms and the remaining ones for the eight
data sets. MAO-SRE and PSO-SRE were the best-ranked

models for half of the data sets. MAO-SRE was statistically
different (i.e., had lower ARs) than PSO-SRE for data sets
D1, D4, and D5. At the same time, PSO-SRE was statistically
different (i.e., had lower ARs) than MAO-SRE for data sets
D6 and D8. No significant differences between MAO-SRE
and PSO-SRE were found for data sets D2 and D3.

All remaining models were significantly different (i.e.,
worse, with higher ARs) than the corresponding best-ranked
algorithm (MAO-SRE or PSO-SRE).
These results suggest that MAO-SRE can be used to
predict the software development effort of a project, considering the following related to development type, development
platform, and programming language type when adjusted
function points are the explanatory variable:

1) Software enhancement projects coded in 3GL and
developed in Mainframe, MidRange, or Multiplatform.
2) New software projects coded in 3GL and developed in
Mainframe or Multiplatform.
3) New or enhancement software projects coded in 4GL
and developed in Multiplatform.

Moreover, the PSO-SRE can also be applied as an alternative
in software enhancement projects coded in 3GL and developed on personal computers due to the good performance
of PSO-SRE when applied to the same data sets used in the
present study [49].
MAO-SRE improves upon previous swarm optimization
methods by enabling rapid convergence, typically within only
500 objective function evaluations, while maintaining a small
population size of 10 individuals. Despite its compact design,
the algorithm does not compromise the capacity to explore the
search space effectively. Instead, it achieves a robust balance
between exploration and exploitation, allowing it to identify
high-quality solutions efficiently. This equilibrium is crucial
in optimization contexts where premature convergence can
lead to suboptimal results.
By leveraging the collective intelligence of the swarm
and using female and male subpopulations, MAO-SRE
enhances diversity during the initial iterations and progressively focuses on fine-tuning the most promising regions of
the search space as the process advances.
Furthermore, this optimization framework is not limited to
the prediction of SRE parameters. Its versatility makes it suitable for broader applications in computational intelligence,
particularly in tuning the architecture and hyperparameters of


VOLUME 13, 2025 207457

Y. Villuendas-Rey et al.: Swarm Intelligence for Predicting Software Development Effort


deep learning models or similar complex tasks. The method’s
efficiency in resource utilization and convergence rate positions it as a promising alternative to traditional optimization
algorithms.

*C. LIMITATIONS AND VALIDITY*

In the following, we summarize the main limitations of our
study, as follows:

1) We could only use eight data sets from the ISBSG
Release 2018 by observing the ISBSG guidelines for
selecting suitable data sets.
2) We could only compare our results with one metaheuristic algorithm (i.e., PSO-SRE), which had been
trained and tested using the same experimental design
as the one followed in the present study.
3) Other factors influence SDEP, such as those related
to software (i.e., experience on similar projects, specialization, or knowledge of developing technology).
However, the ISBSG did not include data regarding
these factors.

4) To be able to compare MAO-SRE in fair conditions
to other metaheuristics, we will need to change the
corresponding metaheuristics to be able to optimize
several equations simultaneously. That is, we need to
modify the internal procedure of the metaheuristics one
by one.

Four possible types of validity threats can be addressed into a
software prediction models field [71] which were addressed
in our study as follows:

1) EXTERNALS
(1) A poor quality in the first SDLC phase depicted in
Figure 1 (i.e., requirements specification) not only provokes
delays in the next SDLC phases and increases the cost of
a software project [72] but also in the context of SDEP.
The explanatory variable used by the MAO-SRE is the size
represented in adjusted function points, which means that the
accuracy of MAO-SRE’s predictions will rely on the accurate
estimation of this variable, which will depend on the product
quality obtained from the first SDLC phase, that is, on a
good specification of requirements of the software project,
and (2) The performance of the MAO-SRE was obtained
observing the ISBSG guidelines, therefore, the performance
of the MAO-SRE will depend of selecting projects having
the same criteria used in the present study, such as, size type,
type of development, development platform, programming
language type, and resource level; unfortunately, we could
not use data sets of those previous related studies included
in Table 2 except one of them [49], once they did not used
the ISBSG, therefore it was impossible to select the data
sets observing the ISBSG suggested criteria, (3) Although
the type of projects were developed into multiple types of
both industry sectors and applications, the application of
MAO-SRE will depend of similar projects used in our study
such as communications, insurance, manufacturing, govern

ment, banking, medical and health care, financial, electronics,
and service industry [67].

2) INTERNAL
We selected the ‘‘A’’ and ‘‘B’’ rankings regarding quality
data once the ISBSG suggested them for statistical analysis;
however, we do not know the statistical criteria followed for
the ISBSG, such that this suggestion has been generated.

3) CONSTRUCT
We transformed the values of both explanatory and dependent
variables using the natural logarithm. Thus, they were not
used in their actual form.

Conclusions: A common concern into the software engineering prediction field is related to the uncertainty [73], [74].
This validity threat does not apply due to our conclusions
have been supported on statistical significance.

**VI. CONCLUSION**

Results after comparing the MAO-SRE performance to those
obtained from the SRE, MLP, SVR, RF, PSO-SRE, and

GA-SRE allow us to conclude that MAO-SRE can be used to

predict, from the project size represented in adjusted function
points, the software development effort of a project selected,
taking into account its development type, development platform, programming language type, and the manner in which
the effort was quantified.
The proposed MAO-SRE can be used for other SDEP
models without restriction on the number of SREs to be

considered. On the one hand, future work will include the
MAO-SRE application in software organizations. On the
other hand, in addition to feature weighting, feature selection
has been performed based on metaheuristic algorithms into
the SDEP field; however, the use of metaheuristic algorithms
for feature selection is reported as scarce in a systematic literature review on SDEP published in 2019 [7], which reports
the use of only three of them: genetic algorithms, PSO, and
Tabu search.

Future work will involve the following issues:

1) In addition to feature weighting, feature selection has
been performed based on metaheuristic algorithms in
the SDEP field; however, the use of metaheuristic algorithms for feature selection is reported as scarce in
a systematic literature review on SDEP published in
2019 [7], which reports the use of only three of them:
genetic algorithms, PSO, and Tabu search. Thus, our
future work will be based on the suggestion of the
authors of the mentioned systematic review, that is,
on the application of algorithms such as ant colony,
wolf, cuckoo, harmony, firefly, and bee searching to
feature selection. Moreover, these algorithms will be
trained and tested using data sets of the most recent
ISBSG release.

2) Explainable models correspond to a recent field into
the software engineering prediction field [75], [76],


207458 VOLUME 13, 2025

Y. Villuendas-Rey et al.: Swarm Intelligence for Predicting Software Development Effort


thus, future work will be focused on proposing models
to predict software quality, including the number of
defects and defect density, as well as to predict whether
the software will fail or not from interpretable prediction models.

**APPENDIX B**

**ABLATION STUDY FOR MAO-SRE**

The effect of population size in MAO-SRE was studied with
a fixed number of 500 evaluations of the objective function.
We tested populations from 10 to 50 individuals, with increments of 10 in each case. Table 16 presents the average MAR
values of five independent executions.
As shown, the increase in the population with a fixed
number of function evaluations degrades the performance of
the algorithm.


**TABLE 16.** MAR prediction accuracies of MAO-SRE with different
population sizes, for 500 evaluations.

The effect of the number of evaluations in MAO-SRE was

studied with a fixed number of 10 individuals. We tested
populations from 100, 250, 500, and 1000 evaluations of
the objective functions. Table 17 presents the average MAR
values of five independent executions. As shown, increasing
the number of evaluations from 500 to 1000 degraded the
performance of MAO-SRE.

**TABLE 17.** MAR prediction accuracies of MAO-SRE with different
numbers of evaluations, for 10 individuals.

We theorize that the increased exploitation mechanism,
resulting from more iterations, leads to overfitting of the SRE
model, thereby degrading its generalization ability. However,
having only 100 evaluations (10 per individual on average)
was not enough for some data sets (d1, d2, d5) where more
evaluations lead to better results.

Based on the studies performed, we consider that an
increased population hinders the exploration and exploitation
of the MAO heuristic, and increasing the number of evaluations leads to overfitting. Therefore, we suggest maintaining
a population such that each individual has between 10 and
50 functional evaluations on average.

YENNY VILLUENDAS-REY received the B.S. and

M.S. degrees in computer science from the University of Ciego de Ávila, Cuba, in 2005 and 2007,
respectively, and the Ph.D. degree in technical sciences from Universidad Central ‘‘Marta Abreu’’

de Las Villas, in 2014.

She has been a Researcher and a Professor with

CIDETEC, Instituto Politécnico Nacional, Mexico, since 2015. Her research interests include data
analysis, hybrid and incomplete data management,
classification, bio-inspired algorithms, and soft computing.
Dr. Villuendas-Rey is a member of the International Association for
Pattern Recognition (ICRP) and the Mexican Artificial Intelligence Society
(SMIA). She was a recipient of the National Researcher System (SNI) Level
II from SECIHTI, Mexico.


CUAUHTÉMOC LÓPEZ-MARTÍN received the

Ph.D. degree in computer science from Centro de
Investigación en Computación, Instituto Politécnico Nacional, Mexico, in 2007.
He is currently a Researcher with the Information Systems Department, Universidad de
Guadalajara, Jalisco, Mexico. He has years of
industry and higher education experience in information system development and software engineering. His research interests include software
prediction techniques, software processes, and statistics applied to software
engineering.
Dr. López-Martín was a recipient of the National Researcher System (SNI)
Level II from SECIHTI, Mexico. Web page: https://dti.cucea.udg.mx/es/
directorio/cuauhtemoclopez-martin

JOSÉ LUIS VELÁZQUEZ-RODRÍGUEZ received
the B.Eng. degree in computer systems engineering from Instituto Politécnico Nacional (ESCOMIPN), Mexico City, Mexico, in 2016, and the M.Sc.
and Ph.D. degrees in computer science from Centro de Investigación en Computación (CIC-IPN),
Mexico City, in 2018 and 2022, respectively.
He carried out a research stay at the University
of Murcia, Spain, in 2018, focusing on bioinformatics applications. Since 2022, he has been a
Data Scientist with Grupo Salinas, Mexico City, where he works on financial
data analytics, and continues the collaboration with CIC-IPN. His awards
and honors include the recognition of his undergraduate thesis as the best
thesis proposal at IPN, in 2015. His research interests include computational
intelligence, machine learning, rough set theory, bioinspired optimization,

CORNELIO YÁÑEZ-MÁRQUEZ received the
bachelor’s degree in physics and mathematics from the Physics and Mathematics Superior School, Instituto Politécnico Nacional (IPN),
Mexico, in 1989, and the M.Sc. and Ph.D. degrees
from the IPN Center for Computing Research
(CIC), in 1995 and 2002, respectively.
He is currently a Research Professor, Titular
C, and the Chief of the Intelligent Computing
Laboratory, CIC, Instituto Politécnico Nacional.
He established the Alpha-Beta Research Group and is the Leader of the
Alpha-Beta models development. He is the author of 30 books and more than
60 scientific articles. His research interests include associative memories,
neural networks, machine learning, and software engineering.
Dr. Yáñez-Márquez was granted the ‘‘Lázaro Cárdenas Award’’ by the
President of the Mexican Republic. He was a recipient of the National
Researcher System (SNI) Level II from SECIHTI, Mexico.
